bp: NANDA is about a future web where software agents do not merely answer questions, but move around networks, act for people or organizations, and cooperate with other agents they did not originally know. In that world, the practical question is not only whether an agent is clever. It is whether another system can find it, know what it is, check who has authority over it, and decide whether it is allowed to participate in a task. The abstract frames this as the missing control layer for the Agentic Web. The comparison to DNS, ICANN, and certificate authorities matters because the ordinary web became usable at scale only after names, delegated responsibility, and identity checks were separated from individual websites. NANDA tries to extend that kind of infrastructure to autonomous AI agents: a way to resolve agents, certify them, attest to their properties, and govern how they compose across devices, edge systems, clouds, organizations, and network boundaries.
wh: The hard part is that an agent is not like a fixed web page sitting at one address. The abstract says agents are becoming autonomous, mobile, and long-lived, which means they may act across devices, edge computers, and cloud services over time. A simple identity check at one moment is not enough if the agent later moves, changes context, or combines with another agent under a different administrative rule. Discovery is also risky: finding an agent is useful only if the discovered agent is the one it claims to be and if its behavior can be governed. Governance adds another tension. No single central owner can manually approve every agent interaction at internet scale, but leaving every organization to invent its own private naming and trust rules prevents safe cooperation. The core difficulty is therefore shared trust without total central control: many parties must coordinate while preserving verifiability, delegated authority, policy compliance, and room for distributed intelligence.
naive: A smart beginner might start by building better individual agents and giving each one a public profile: name, owner, capabilities, and a list of policies it promises to follow. That fails because a promise written in a profile is not the same as a checkable trust chain. Another beginner move would be to define an agent-to-agent messaging protocol, assuming safe cooperation will follow once agents can talk. The abstract explicitly says NANDA is not focused on that. Communication rules do not answer who the agent is, who certified it, whether its current state matches its certified state, or whether it may cross a particular policy boundary. A third shortcut is to centralize all approval, but that clashes with the abstract's goal of coordination across networks without centralized control.
ap: The central move is to treat agent trust as infrastructure rather than as a feature inside each agent. NANDA borrows the shape of web trust: names that can be resolved, authorities that can delegate responsibility, roots of trust that anchor the chain, and certificates or attestations that let other systems verify claims. In plain terms, it asks the Agentic Web to keep a separate public control layer. That layer says how an agent can be found, which authority stands behind it, what claims have been certified, and what policies govern its use. The abstract's important distinction is that NANDA is not trying to invent every agent or every conversation protocol. It is trying to make agents verifiable, discoverable, policy-compliant, and safely composable when they cross organizational and network borders. The mechanism is therefore less like writing a smarter worker and more like building the registry, identity office, and rule-checking desk that many workers can rely on.
mech: The input to NANDA's imagined system is an agent that needs to be used, discovered, or combined with other agents. First, the agent needs a name or identifier that can be resolved, meaning another party can turn a request for that agent into a trustworthy reference rather than a guess from search results or hearsay. Second, the agent needs some authority chain. A root of trust anchors the system, while delegated authorities can certify agents within their own domains, much as web trust lets responsibility pass from a global root to more local certificate authorities. Third, the agent carries certified claims: who controls it, what class of agent it is, what rules it is expected to follow, and possibly what environment or version it represents. Fourth, attestation provides a check that the agent being contacted still matches the certified claim, rather than being an impostor or altered copy. Fifth, discovery uses these records to let systems find suitable agents without treating every found agent as equally safe. Finally, governance policies decide whether composition is allowed: if agent A from one organization wants to work with agent B from another, the control plane supplies machine-checkable facts about identity, authority, and compliance before cooperation proceeds. The output is not a finished task answer. It is a trust decision and a routable, verifiable agent reference that other systems can use.
math: The main mathematical ideas are naming, graph-like authority chains, verification, and constrained composition. Naming is the act of mapping a human or system request onto a unique referent. The danger it avoids is ambiguity: two agents may use similar names, or one agent may pretend to be another. Resolution turns the name into a specific target through a controlled lookup process. Delegated authority has the shape of a directed chain: one trusted place grants limited trust to another, which may certify a narrower set of agents. The useful question is not whether everyone trusts everyone, but whether there is a path of acceptable responsibility from a root to the agent being checked. Certification and attestation are verification ideas. A certificate says an authority vouches for a claim; attestation says the current object still matches some expected property. Governance adds constraints: before two agents compose, the system must check whether their identities, policies, and boundaries satisfy rules. This is a constraint problem in everyday terms: among many possible agent interactions, allow only those whose trust chain and policy facts fit. The tradeoff is openness versus control. More open discovery makes cooperation easier, but without measured verification and rule checks it also makes impersonation, unsafe composition, and policy violations easier.
dots: This paper sits at the infrastructure end of the repo's LLM agents and tool-use family. Many neighboring papers ask how an agent chooses tools, retrieves evidence, remembers context, or avoids poisoned tool descriptions. NANDA asks a deeper web-level question that comes before a single tool call: how does the network know which agents and authorities deserve to be part of the action chain at all? It also connects to the misinformation and trust family, where the recurring problem is replacing unsupported confidence with inspectable evidence. Here the evidence is not a citation, video provenance record, or fact-checking source, but a resolvable identity, certificate, attestation, and policy record for an agent. Finally, it belongs near privacy, federated, and security work because it is about crossing boundaries. The abstract's focus on administrative and network boundaries matches the broader repo pattern: useful cooperation requires sharing enough signal to coordinate while keeping identity, policy, and authority constraints explicit.
ww: The mechanism should help because it separates three problems that otherwise get tangled together. An individual agent can focus on doing work. A communication protocol can focus on message exchange. NANDA's control layer focuses on whether the parties to the exchange can be named, found, verified, certified, and governed. That separation is why the DNS and certificate-authority analogy is strong in the abstract: the web did not require every website user to personally inspect every server operator. It created common lookup and trust machinery that many independent actors could use. For agents, the same shape is valuable because autonomy increases the cost of mistaken trust. If an agent can act across devices and clouds for a long time, then a wrong identity or missing policy check can propagate through many actions. Resolution reduces confusion about what is being contacted. Certification gives a source of responsibility. Attestation reduces the risk that a certified name hides an altered object. Delegated authority lets local domains enforce their own rules while still taking part in a larger network.
po: The payoff is a path toward an Agentic Web where agents are not just reachable, but governable. The abstract claims NANDA provides a systems-level control plane for agent resolvability, certification, attestation, and discovery. That buys the ability to verify agents before use, compose them more safely across organizations, and enforce policy expectations at internet scale. The result is not a better model architecture or a new agent conversation language. It is a shared trust and governance layer meant to support distributed intelligence, programmable trust, and coordination without putting every decision under one central operator.
limits: The abstract is a systems vision, not evidence of a completed deployment or measured reliability. It does not prove that NANDA's naming rules, certification process, attestation checks, or governance policies can resist every impersonation, compromise, policy conflict, or authority failure. The DNS and certificate-authority analogy is useful, but those systems also have weaknesses: mistaken certificates, concentrated trust, stale records, and governance disputes. NANDA must assume that roots of trust and delegated authorities are themselves accountable, that agent properties can be attested meaningfully, and that policies can be written clearly enough for machines to check. The abstract also does not specify revocation, dispute handling, incentives, or the cost of operating the control plane.
